title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial to measure whether constrained prompting plus a deterministic generate→verify→repair loop (≤1 repair) increases deterministic-verifier semantic correctness when translating operator natural-language intents into low-level device configurations. Design: N=150 synthetic intents (deterministic generator), execution semantics = shared_initial_candidate, model = gpt-5-mini, deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, one initial generation per intent reused across baseline and guarded conditions, guarded pipeline permitted at most one repair call. Results (artifact-grounded): baseline = 149/150 (99.333%); guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.006667 (≈0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Provider accounting: completed episodes = 300; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations = 1. Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus and under shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded workflow produced a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over a near-ceiling baseline; we emphasize the methodological lesson that preregistered NetOps trials require baseline-calibration pilots to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate preregistered power assumptions. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the supplied execution bundle and referenced by the execution manifest.

sections.introduction: Natural-language intent interfaces aim to let operators express desired network changes as free text while automation translates those intents to device configurations. Prior work documents frequent syntactic errors, omissions, and sequence/semantic violations in single-pass LLM outputs that can produce unsafe states if applied directly [1][2][3]. A common mitigation is a generate→verify→repair architecture: an LLM produces a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks intent-level invariants, and an automated repair (or human gate) corrects violations before execution [2][4]. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory trial to ask: does constrained prompting (structured templates with explicit semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase deterministic-verifier semantic-correctness of NL→configuration translation versus an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? The run reported here (study_cand_2026_b2_v1) was preregistered and frozen before any model outputs were observed. Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, artifactized paired trial using a deterministic synthetic corpus (N=150 paired intents) and an explicit shared_initial_candidate execution semantic; (2) artifact-backed numeric outcomes showing a near-ceiling baseline (149/150) and minimal guarded gain (150/150); (3) a methodological recommendation—baseline calibration pilots are necessary in preregistered NetOps trials to avoid ceiling effects and preserve inferential validity.
sections.related_work: Empirical and survey studies show that NL→configuration translation is challenging: free-text prompts frequently omit required steps or produce incorrect sequencing, producing modest semantic-correctness rates on heterogeneous task banks [1]. Systems incorporating deterministic verification and verifier-guided repair report practical correctness improvements for IaC and configuration-repair tasks, but effect sizes depend on baseline competence, verifier expressiveness, repair budget, and sampling semantics [2][3]. Fast symbolic/network-verification engines (NetKAT/KATch family and related tools) can serve as deterministic oracles for reachability and policy checks and provide diagnostic counterexamples useful for automated repair, although tooling varies in supported protocols and scale [5]. Security analyses of agentic, tool-augmented pipelines demonstrate claim-to-action vulnerabilities (prompt-injection, conversion of false textual claims into harmful actions) and motivate explicit conservative gating and auditable verifier verdicts [4]. Our trial intentionally enforced three operational knobs identified in prior work: (a) shared_initial_candidate semantics so baseline and guarded contrasts reuse the identical initial LLM sample per intent; (b) a tight repair budget (≤1 repair) consistent with low-latency operational constraints; and (c) a deterministic verifier as strict binary oracle. These choices bound the observable marginal benefit of guarded repair under the preregistered estimand and explain how published larger effects can coexist with our bounded result when different sampling or repair regimes are evaluated [2][3][5][6].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses mapping. The study was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1 with a frozen analysis plan (primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The preregistration conceptually listed three conditions (A: baseline free-text prompt, B: constrained template prompt, C: constrained + verifier-feedback). Reviewer-required clarification (explicit and artifact-backed): the executed and archived confirmatory contrast is C vs A under shared_initial_candidate semantics; the constrained-only condition B was not executed as an independent first-pass sample in this run and therefore no B-vs-A or C-vs-B confirmatory contrasts appear in the archived analysis artifacts. Mapping: preregistered H1/H2 corresponded to constrained vs baseline and guarded vs constrained in the conceptual design, but the actual, adapter-enforced, archived primary test is guarded (C) vs baseline (A) using the same sampled initial candidate per intent. No post-preregistration analytic or design changes were made after observing outcomes; the analysis follows the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor.

Execution semantics and adapter enforcement. Execution semantics were shared_initial_candidate: for each intent the adapter produced exactly one initial model generation and reused that candidate for both baseline and guarded paired evaluations. The guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call only if the deterministic verifier failed the initial candidate. The adapter enforced these constraints and produced provider-level accounting: stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 150, repair: 1} and model_calls_used = 151. Declared model and sampling: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" (provider record: openai_responses) and the archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset). Because no numeric temperature or fixed random seed was enforced, independent API sessions may be nondeterministic; this nondeterminism was anticipated in the preregistration and materially affects which estimand is identified by independent-sampling vs shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Corpus, verifier, and scoring. Confirmatory tasks were deterministically generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and stratified across four intent families (reachability/isolation, ACL-like access changes, VLAN/MTU sequence changes, uplink switchover). Topologies were constrained to small, verifier-capable networks (4–32 nodes) to ensure oracle coverage. The deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) applying the full_intent_constraint_validation rule; it returned a boolean pass/fail plus normalized_configuration and diagnostic fields (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes). Primary endpoint = verifier pass (binary). Inclusion/exclusion rules, retry policy (one retry for provider timeouts), and complete-pair treatment (complete_pair_primary) were applied exactly as preregistered. Mapping unit-tests for translation to verifier inputs were run before batch execution and passed; no confirmatory exclusions occurred.

Primary analysis. The primary analysis used an exact two-sided McNemar test on the paired contingency table (n_11, n_10, n_01, n_00) and a paired-bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Multiplicity: the preregistered primary contrast is single and two secondary contrasts were specified conceptually, but under shared_initial_candidate enforcement the archived run only produced the paired counts for guarded vs baseline; therefore secondary confirmatory contrasts are not available from the archived confirmatory artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit. The run completed as planned: completed_episode_count = 300 and complete_pair_count = 150. Provider-call accounting: model_calls_used = 151; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 151; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 151. Stage-level counts recorded by the adapter: shared_initial_generation = 150 and repair = 1. Contamination checks and mapping unit-tests passed; contamination_summary.csv is empty.

Primary numeric outcomes. The paired contingency (guarded × baseline) was n_11 = 149, n_10 = 1, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Per-condition success counts: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (≈0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). These numbers are reported verbatim from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).

Repair diagnostics and revision counts. Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); that single repair converted one initially failing candidate to a verifier-pass. Median revision iterations in guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). Representative validator traces for tasks 000001–000006 are archived and show parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, and valid flags consistent with the deterministic verifier behavior documented in the methods.

Representative example. Task-000001 (generator_seed = 1) intent: "Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up. Do not modify any other interface." Shared-initial response and both condition responses matched the expected four-command sequence; validator diagnostics: parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, observed_touched_field_count = 3, valid = true. The shared-initial candidate and normalized_configuration are archived in the execution bundle.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and power invalidation. The preregistered power calculation targeted detection of an absolute +15 percentage-point improvement with N=150 under conservative discordant assumptions. The observed baseline_success_rate = 0.9933 produced a near-ceiling baseline, leaving little headroom for a detectable absolute improvement and drastically reducing the number of informative discordant pairs. Concretely, with n_11 = 149 and a single discordant pair (n_10 = 1), the paired analysis carries minimal information about marginal conversion rates; hence the exact McNemar p = 1.0 and wide inferential indeterminacy relative to the preregistered target. Methodological implication: preregistered NetOps trials should include a short baseline-calibration pilot (e.g., 20–40 tasks from the planned generator and prompt style) to estimate baseline competence and then set confirmatory N or task difficulty so that power assumptions remain realistic.

Sampling semantics and estimand interpretation. The shared_initial_candidate execution semantic makes the guarded−baseline contrast a pure marginal-repair estimand (the same initial sampled candidate is evaluated under baseline and guarded conditions). Alternative semantics—independent per-condition sampling or multi-draw ensembles—answer different operational questions (expected pass rate under independent pipelines, or cost–benefit of resampling). Independent sampling or larger repair budgets can increase discordant-pair counts (n_10+n_01) and statistical power, but at higher model-call and latency cost. Practitioners must choose sampling semantics that match deployment constraints and incorporate model-call budgets into power planning.

Operational implications beyond binary pass/fail. Deterministic guarded pipelines provide richer operational observability even when marginal verifier-pass gains are small: the verifier produces normalized_configuration strings and explicit violation_codes (missing-step, order-violation) that accelerate triage, support auditable change records, and enable targeted automated repair policies. The archived validator traces illustrate such diagnostic outputs that can reduce human review time despite minimal change in the binary pass metric.

Threats to validity and scope. Internal validity: adapter-enforced budgets and provider audits mitigate cross-condition leakage; mapping unit-tests reduced parse/translation failures. Construct validity: deterministic verifier pass is a proxy for semantic correctness and depends on mapping code and verifier coverage; uncovered verifier gaps would bias measurement. External validity: results derive from a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) on a synthetic corpus limited to small topologies (4–32 nodes) and do not generalize to production WANs or other models. Security: this trial did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection; adversary-driven experiments are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities. Conclusion validity: the mismatch between preregistered detectable-effect assumptions and observed baseline underscores the need for pilot calibration.
sections.conclusion: On a preregistered synthetic corpus and under shared_initial_candidate semantics, constrained prompting plus a single verifier-guided repair produced a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant change in deterministic-verifier pass rate (baseline 149/150 → guarded 150/150; absolute difference ≈0.67 pp; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered NetOps trials must include baseline-calibration pilots to avoid ceiling effects and preserve power. Operationally, verifier-guided pipelines yield diagnostic artifacts that can improve auditability and triage even when binary-pass gains are small. Evaluating independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, model diversity, and production-scale topologies remains future work and should be approached with preregistered baseline calibration and cost-aware power planning.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic validator pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
